title: Birbal and the Beggar Woman
summary: An old beggar woman refuses alms thrown into the dust with contempt by a wealthy nobleman. Birbal shows Akbar why respect is greater than charity.
full_text:
Outside the grand Jama Masjid in Agra, an elderly, blind beggar woman named Amma sat quietly, never shouting or pleading, holding out a modest clay bowl.

A wealthy and haughty nobleman, Nawab Safdar Jung, passed by on his magnificent grey stallion. Tossing a shiny silver rupee coin carelessly from his saddle, the coin missed the bowl, landed in a filthy puddle of street mud, and splashed dirty water over the old woman's face and cotton sari.

The nobleman sneered: 'Pick it up from the mud, old crone! That silver coin can buy you bread for a month!'

To the amazement of the crowd, the blind woman did not grovel in the mud. She wiped the dirty water from her face with her sleeve, left the silver coin lying untouched in the puddle, and said in a calm, clear voice:

'Keep your silver, Nawab Sahib. My hunger is only for bread, which will pass in a day. But your soul is starved of human decency, which will torment you for eternity. I am poor, but I am not a dog to eat from your insults.'

The incident caused a stir in the bazaar and was reported to Emperor Akbar.

Akbar was puzzled: 'Why did a starving beggar woman refuse a silver rupee simply because it fell in the mud? Money is money!'

Birbal replied with profound solemnity:

'Sire, charity given without respect is not a blessing; it is an assault upon the soul of the poor.

'When a man throws money into the dust with contempt, he is not helping the beggar; he is merely feeding his own disgusting vanity.

'The old woman refused the coin because her dignity was worth more to her than bread. A noble heart can beat inside rags, just as a cowardly, cruel heart can beat beneath silk.'

Akbar was deeply moved. The next morning, Akbar and Birbal walked quietly to the mosque. The Emperor knelt down in the dust, placed two gold mohurs gently into the old woman's hands, and bowed his head, saying: 'Mother, accept this humble gift from a son who honors your noble spirit.'

The old woman touched Akbar's brow, blessed him with tears of joy, and Akbar commended Birbal for teaching the court the true sanctity of human dignity.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Birbal and the Beggar Woman"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?

By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
